common_name: Holy Grail Hibiscus (Darkest-Foliage Red-Flowered Hardy Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Holy Grail carries some of the darkest, near-black foliage of any hardy hibiscus, paired with huge deep red flowers.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun, providing consistent water throughout the growing season since hardy hibiscus is naturally a wetland-edge plant. Holy Grail bears some of the darkest, most saturated near-black purple foliage available in the Summerific breeding line, a dramatic backdrop for enormous, deep velvety-red flowers that open in steady succession from midsummer into fall. Like other hardy hibiscus, each flower lasts only a single day but is quickly replaced by the next bud, keeping the plant in nearly continuous bloom for weeks at a stretch. It dies back completely to the ground each winter and emerges quite late in spring, often not until several weeks after other perennials have leafed out, so mark its location to avoid disturbing the dormant crown. Watch for Japanese beetles, which can heavily skeletonize the foliage and flowers where present, and cut old stems to the ground in late winter before new growth begins.

common_name: Starry Starry Night Hibiscus (Dark Foliage White-and-Red Star-Patterned Hardy Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Starry Starry Night pairs dark purple-black foliage with white flowers marked by a bold red central eye and fine red veining radiating outward.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun, providing consistent water throughout the growing season since hardy hibiscus is naturally a wetland-edge plant. Starry Starry Night combines deep, near-black purple foliage with huge white flowers centered on a bold red eye, with fine red veining radiating out across the petals like the rays of a star, a striking high-contrast combination against the dark leaves. It flowers in a steady procession of enormous blooms from midsummer into fall, each lasting a single day before being replaced by the next. Like other hardy hibiscus it dies back completely to the ground each winter, emerging quite late in spring, so mark the crown's location to avoid accidental damage while other perennials are already up. Watch for Japanese beetle damage on the foliage and flowers, and cut old stems to the ground in late winter before new growth resumes.

common_name: French Vanilla Hibiscus (Enormous Creamy-White Hardy Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; French Vanilla bears huge, creamy vanilla-white flowers on a well-branched, compact plant, without the dark foliage of many newer hardy hibiscus introductions.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun, providing consistent water throughout the growing season since hardy hibiscus is naturally a wetland-edge plant. French Vanilla bears enormous, softly creamy vanilla-white flowers over clean green, deeply lobed foliage on a compact, well-branched plant, a gentler, more restrained look than the near-black-leaved, high-contrast cultivars now common in the hardy hibiscus trade. Its dinner-plate-sized blooms open in a steady succession from midsummer into fall, each lasting only a day but replaced continuously by new buds, and the pale color pairs easily with almost any companion planting. Like other hardy hibiscus it dies back completely to the ground each winter and emerges late in spring, so mark its location to avoid disturbing the dormant crown early in the season. Watch for Japanese beetles on the foliage and flowers, and cut old stems back in late winter before new growth begins.

common_name: Grace Smokebush (Large-Leaved Purple Hybrid Smoke Tree)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained to dry, average to lean soil in full sun; Grace is a hybrid between the European and American smoke trees, larger and more vigorous than typical Cotinus coggygria cultivars.

directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, average to lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; this hybrid smoke tree tolerates rocky, sandy soils where many flowering shrubs struggle. Grace is a cross between the European smoke tree and the American smoke tree, combining larger, more translucent wine-purple leaves with a taller, more vigorous, tree-like habit than most Cotinus coggygria cultivars, and its summer display of airy, pink-tinged smoke-like flower panicles is correspondingly larger and showier. The purple foliage takes on brilliant scarlet-orange fall color before dropping, giving the plant a second season of strong ornamental interest. It tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil once established, needing only an occasional thinning cut in late winter to maintain an open, well-shaped form; hard pruning each spring produces larger leaves but sacrifices the summer smoke display, so choose a pruning approach based on which effect matters more in a given planting.

common_name: Velvet Cloak Smokebush (Deep Purple Compact Smoke Tree)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained to dry, average to lean soil in full sun; Velvet Cloak is valued for holding a deeper, more consistent purple foliage color through summer heat than older purple smokebush cultivars.

directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, average to lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; like other smokebush cultivars it tolerates rocky, sandy, and drought-prone sites better than richer, consistently moist soil. Velvet Cloak produces deep, rich wine-purple foliage that resists fading to green or bronze through summer heat better than many older purple-leaved smokebush selections, holding strong color from spring leaf-out into fall, when it turns brilliant scarlet-orange before dropping. Its billowing, airy, pink-purple summer flower panicles create the characteristic smoky haze that gives the plant its common name, standing out well against the dark foliage. It tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil once established, needing only occasional thinning in late winter to maintain an open, well-branched form and remove any dead or crossing wood.
